name: Fatima Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Fatima, and thank you for your time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you describe a normal day at work for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the pig unit at Ashby Grange. Two hundred and fifty sows, farrowing to finishing, plus about a hundred and forty hectares of barley and maize that mostly goes back into the feed. The owner inherited the place, he's a retired accountant who lives two hours away, so day to day it's me and three staff. I'm in the farrowing house at six checking the new litters, then it's rounds, feed, paperwork, and some kind of argument with the ventilation system.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy making the numbers work. Last year I got our piglets weaned per sow up by almost two, which is a big deal in pigs. What's hard is the pay, which is low for what I do, and being on call. My partner Leon's an electrician, self-employed, so his money comes in lumps, and we've had a couple of months where we've both been watching the bank app like a weather radar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, that's roughly what I expected. I use one of those AI chat tools now and then to double-check a feed ration or draft a letter to the owner, and that's helpful, but it was never going to run a pig unit. At work I'd just say, right, back to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job is safe and my pay is still low, so nothing changes. The bit that worries me about this farm was never AI, it's the owner deciding one day to sell up. That risk is the same either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. I'd keep using the AI tool for the odd ration check. I'd try to get the owner to agree a bonus tied to piglet numbers, because that's something I can actually move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored by the whole thing, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the owner selling up worries you more. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard to say. He's sixty-eight and his kids live abroad. Every time he rings, I wonder if this is the call where he says he's had an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a bonus on piglet numbers mean for you, in money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could get even a few hundred a quarter, that would be the difference between saving nothing and saving something. We're trying to get a deposit together for a house, very slowly.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, that's what I expected, because AI was never going to run a pig unit. At work I'd say right, back to it.
S0.think: It means my job is safe and my pay is still low. The real risk on this farm is the owner selling up, and that's the same either way.
S0.do: Keeps using an AI chat tool now and then for feed rations and letters. Tries to agree a quarterly bonus with the owner tied to piglet numbers.
S0.feel: Calm and a little bored by the whole topic.
S0.quote: Every time he rings, I wonder if this is the call where he says he's had an offer.
S0.fieldNote: Her focus is on the owner's age and plans, which she sees as the real risk regardless of AI. She thinks in numbers and wants pay linked to the results she controls. She mentions saving for a house deposit, which frames her later choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Okay, next picture. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how we work, and the sensible thing is to get ahead of it. In pigs a lot is already automated, feed lines, climate control, so it's not new to us. I'd say at work, let's see what actually works in other units first, then copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's a mixed bag for me. Cameras that spot a sick pig early, I'd love that. But if the owner sees he can run the unit with two people instead of four, I'm the expensive one, even on my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the regional pig producers' day in March and see who's using the camera systems. Once a couple of units have had them a year, I'd put a proposal to the owner, with numbers, and make sure I'm the one running it. And Leon and I would start putting a bit aside every month, even a hundred.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky, just that feeling of 'I need to be ready for this'.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make sure you're the one running it. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By writing the proposal myself, with the costs and the savings. If I bring him the robot with a spreadsheet, I'm the manager. If someone else does, I'm a cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, mostly. He's been doing the washing and the moving for fifteen years and he's brilliant with the pigs, but he doesn't do screens. I'd try to keep a role for him, but I can't promise anything.

S1.say: I'd say it'll change how we work and the sensible thing is to get ahead of it. In pigs a lot is already automated, so I'd suggest copying what works in other units.
S1.think: It's a mixed bag: cameras that spot sick pigs early would be great, but if the owner can run the unit with two people, I'm the expensive one.
S1.do: Attends the regional pig producers' day in March to see camera systems in use, and writes a costed proposal to the owner once other units have used them for a year. Starts saving about a hundred a month with her partner.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a sense that she needs to be ready.
S1.quote: If I bring him the robot with a spreadsheet, I'm the manager. If someone else does, I'm a cost.
S1.fieldNote: She sees automation as normal in pigs and plans to own the change by writing the business case herself. She's steady: she wants proof from other units first. She worries about a long-serving worker who doesn't use screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next three are bigger. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going much too fast, and the government needs to slow it down or at least put a safety net in. I'd say it at work and to friends. I'm not a big poster online but I might share something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the pig unit becomes one robot system and a vet on a screen, and that's me and the team gone within the two years. The owner would probably sell to a big integrator. With about three weeks of savings, that's frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, Leon and I would stop the house deposit and use it as an emergency fund. I'd start looking for anything nearby that still needs a person, maybe the feed mill or the meat inspection side, though I don't know if those last either. Once it arrives, if there's government support I'd take it, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do two years of warning actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very little. Two years is about four batches of pigs from birth to sale. By the time I'd finished a course, the job I trained for would already have gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Leon's work as an electrician. Would that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, maybe. Somebody has to wire up all these robots at first. But if it's really AGI, robots wire robots soon enough. So I'd lean on him for a year or so, and then I'd honestly have no idea.

S2.say: I'd say it's going too fast and the government needs to slow it down or build a safety net. I'd say it at work and maybe share something online.
S2.think: The pig unit becomes one robot system and a vet on a screen, and my team and I are gone within two years. With about three weeks of savings, that's frightening.
S2.do: Turns the house deposit into an emergency fund and looks for any nearby work that still needs a person, such as the feed mill. Leans on her partner's electrical work for a while and takes government support once AGI arrives.
S2.quote: By the time I'd finished a course, the job I trained for would already have gone.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline wipes out her usual tool, a careful business case. She judges that two years is too short to retrain and says so plainly. She's pragmatic about public support, with no hesitation about taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, a bit slower. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. I'd tell the other pig managers at the producers' group, let's not wait to be told. Sensible planning, that's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years makes me think about what Leon and I could do together. He's an electrician, I know the livestock systems inside out. There might be two or three years of good work installing and fixing these things on farms before they fix themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do an evening course in electrical installation, so I can work with Leon. I'd ask the owner to put the camera system in now and let me run it, to learn it. We'd keep saving, maybe a hundred and fifty a month, but we'd hold off on the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. That's better than lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Working with your partner. How do you think that would go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, we'd probably argue about tidiness in the van. He thinks like a wire and I think like a pig, and you need both to set up a farm robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there might be two or three years of work. And after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After that I don't know. I'd be thirty-two, maybe thirty-three. I'd hope something else comes along, but I can't plan that far with any honesty.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan if people start now. I'd tell the other pig managers in the producers' group not to wait to be told.
S3.think: Five years makes me think about working with my partner, since he's an electrician and I know the livestock systems. There might be two or three years of good work installing these things.
S3.do: Takes an evening course in electrical installation in the first year and asks the owner to install camera monitoring now so she can learn it. Saves about a hundred and fifty a month and holds off on buying a house.
S3.feel: Anxious but with a plan, which beats lying awake.
S3.quote: He thinks like a wire and I think like a pig, and you need both to set up a farm robot.
S3.fieldNote: The middle timeline turns her pragmatism into a joint plan with her partner. She's candid that the plan only covers a few years and she can't see beyond it. Her line about wires and pigs captures how the two skills fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time and we should use it sensibly, no panic. I'd say the government should fund training and the industry should help. Pretty middle of the road, like most of what I say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough that it's more of a career question than a crisis. I'd be thirty-seven, with time to move into something steady. I'm not sure what, but I'm not scared yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the unit and push to bring in the monitoring kit in the next couple of years, so I learn it properly. Over five years I'd go for a qualification in farm systems or animal health tech, part-time. And Leon and I would probably go ahead with the house, but somewhere in a bigger town rather than out here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the back, but mostly fine. Like a long-range forecast, you take note.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a bigger town rather than out here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in ten years, I doubt there'll be much work in a village like ours. I'd rather buy a smaller house where there are jobs than a nice one surrounded by fields that run themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not scared yet. What would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the owner sold early, in year two or three. Then it's suddenly the five-year picture again, with the clock running. So I'd keep an eye on him, and on any big companies sniffing around.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time to use sensibly, with no panic. The government should fund training and industry should help.
S4.think: Ten years makes it a career question, not a crisis. I'd be thirty-seven with time to move into something steady, and I'm not scared yet.
S4.do: Keeps running the unit and brings in monitoring kit over the next couple of years to learn it properly. Works towards a part-time qualification in farm systems or animal health technology over five years, and buys a house with her partner in a bigger town.
S4.feel: Uneasy at the back of her mind but mostly fine.
S4.quote: I'd rather buy a smaller house where there are jobs than a nice one surrounded by fields that run themselves.
S4.fieldNote: She treats the ten-year picture as a career plan rather than an emergency. Her choice of a bigger town is a clear-eyed bet on where work will be. She names a specific trigger, an early sale of the farm, that would turn this back into a crisis.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because everything I'm good at, planning and numbers, needs time. What would help is a bit of income support for the gap and short, paid courses that actually lead to a job, not just a certificate. I can plan for almost anything if someone gives me the dates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about animal welfare. If a pig unit runs itself, who notices the sow that's just a bit off? I'd want someone to keep asking that.

headlineQuote: I can plan for almost anything if someone gives me the dates.
portrait: Fatima Nakamura is a 27-year-old who runs a 250-sow pig unit and its feed crops for an absentee owner, with a degree, low pay and about three weeks of savings, saving slowly for a house with her electrician partner Leon. She's pragmatic and in the middle politically, uses AI tools now and then, and likes change once she's seen it work elsewhere. If AI is hype she's calm, and with steady change she'd write the business case for camera monitoring herself. AGI in two years alarms her because it leaves no time for her careful planning. With five or ten years she builds a plan with Leon around installing farm systems and moves towards a bigger town.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because her strengths, planning and numbers, need time.
whatWouldHelp: Income support for the gap and short paid courses that lead to an actual job.
